items.item: an LSN is a byte offset into the WAL, increasing monotonically with each new record, and comparable to measure the volume of WAL data between two of them

at.step: Reveal: a real log position, read directly off this sandbox's own cluster

items.item: wal_sync_method's real options include fdatasync, fsync, and an open_datasync option built on the O_DSYNC open flag

at.step: Reveal: three real ways to force a write out, and which one this sandbox actually uses

items.item: commit_delay can improve group commit throughput by letting more transactions share one WAL flush, at the cost of added per-commit latency

at.step: Reveal: the write-ahead rule, and a measured trick that bends it without breaking it

items.item: full-page writes log a page's entire content on its first modification after a checkpoint, because an interrupted page write can leave a mix of old and new data

at.step: Reveal: a torn page's real defense, measured triggering exactly once per checkpoint

items.item: a disk write happens in fixed-size sectors, and a crash partway through can leave some sectors written and others not

at.step: Predict: does a torn page mean a write always lands as all-or-nothing?

items.item: PostgreSQL periodically writes full page images to WAL before modifying the actual page, so a partially-written page can be restored from WAL during crash recovery

at.step: Reveal: a torn page's real defense, measured triggering exactly once per checkpoint

items.item: in 2018, multiple Linux kernel versions were found to lose or misreport fsync errors, so a buffer could be marked clean after a failed write and discarded under memory pressure

at.step: Reveal: a real, documented lesson a failed force-out taught the hard way

items.item: PostgreSQL's real fix, backpatched across five release lines, is to PANIC on an fsync failure rather than retry it

at.step: Reveal: a real, documented lesson a failed force-out taught the hard way

items.item: InnoDB writes a page to its own doublewrite buffer first and only writes it to its final destination once that buffer copy is safely flushed, recovering a half-written page by checking the buffer's own copy

at.step: Reveal: a different engine's own defense against the identical torn-page problem

items.item: The write-ahead rule isn't just 'log things' — it specifically requires the log record to be durable (flushed) before the changed data page itself is written back, which is the exact ordering this topic's own LSN measurement and group-commit measurement both depend on.

at.step: Reveal: the write-ahead rule, and a measured trick that bends it without breaking it

items.item: An LSN is useful precisely because it's comparable: replication and recovery both work by asking 'how far ahead is this LSN of that one,' not by inspecting log contents directly.

at.step: Reveal: a real log position, read directly off this sandbox's own cluster

items.item: Group commit doesn't weaken the write-ahead rule at all — every one of the grouped transactions still waits for its own flush to actually complete before it's reported as committed; it only reduces how many separate flushes that waiting costs in total.

at.step: Reveal: the write-ahead rule, and a measured trick that bends it without breaking it

items.item: A torn page is a physical-layer problem, not a software bug: the database's own page size (commonly 8 kB) is written in multiple smaller physical sector writes, and nothing above that layer can assume all of them land together.

at.step: Predict: does a torn page mean a write always lands as all-or-nothing?

items.item: Full-page writes only need to fire once per page per checkpoint cycle, because WAL replay always starts from a checkpoint anyway — logging the full page again on a second change to the same page before the next checkpoint would be pure waste.

at.step: Reveal: a torn page's real defense, measured triggering exactly once per checkpoint

items.item: fsync, fdatasync and the O_DSYNC-based option all answer the same question (force this out to real storage) at different costs: fdatasync skips flushing metadata that doesn't affect how the data reads back, which is why it's the faster default on the platforms that support it correctly.

at.step: Reveal: three real ways to force a write out, and which one this sandbox actually uses

items.item: InnoDB's doublewrite buffer and Postgres's full-page writes solve the identical problem (recovering from a torn page) with opposite trade-offs: InnoDB pays a second physical write up front on every flush, while Postgres pays extra WAL volume only on a page's first change after a checkpoint.

at.step: Reveal: a different engine's own defense against the identical torn-page problem

items.item: The 2018 fsyncgate lesson generalizes past Postgres: any system that calls fsync and trusts a success return value was exposed, because the kernel's own error-reporting contract at the time didn't guarantee a caller could ever reliably learn that a write had actually failed.

at.step: Reveal: a real, documented lesson a failed force-out taught the hard way

items.item: Crashing on a failed fsync looks drastic, but the alternative is worse: once a caller can't trust that 'fsync succeeded' means the data is actually durable, the only state anyone can still trust is whatever a full crash-and-replay from the last known-good checkpoint reconstructs.

at.step: Reveal: a real, documented lesson a failed force-out taught the hard way

items.item: wal_sync_method is a per-cluster configuration choice, not a fixed property of the database engine itself — the same Postgres binary can be told to use any of several real system calls depending on what the underlying platform and filesystem actually support correctly.

This topic is the durability layer every later Chapter 5 topic assumes: checkpoints bound how far back a crash recovery must replay this exact log, B-tree page splits and MVCC version writes are themselves WAL records before they're anything else.
